tldr: A real-time method that directly lifts large visual foundation model features onto 3D point clouds, predicting an object's 6D pose, metric size, and complete 3D shape in a single forward pass at 28 FPS.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of F2G-Pose. RADIOv2.5 features are extracted from cropped RGB images, lifted onto partial point clouds, and tokenized for local geometry using DGCNN. A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformer then acquires an object-level representation, simultaneously predicting pose, size, and camera-frame shape completion in a single feed-forward pass.
overview:
When robots grasp and manipulate unfamiliar objects, category-level 6D object pose estimation—recovering an object's 3D pose and real-world metric size without instance-specific CAD models—is essential. However, the task has long suffered from strong ambiguities caused by partial observations, intra-class shape variations, and symmetries, which prevent a unique solution. Existing deterministic approaches rely on intermediate mappings to a canonical coordinate frame, making them prone to error propagation under occlusions or missing data. On the other hand, recent generative approaches such as diffusion models sample multiple candidates and filter them out post-hoc, leading to heavy inference latency that cannot keep up with real-time control.

To address this, the authors developed F2G-Pose, a framework that directly regresses pose, size, and 3D shape in a single feed-forward pass without any sampling or intermediate coordinate alignment. The key idea is to directly lift the rich semantic features of a vision foundation model (RADIOv2.5) onto observed point clouds, encode local geometry with DGCNN, and flexibly integrate shapes across diverse categories using a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformer. Furthermore, by jointly training camera-frame 3D shape completion as an auxiliary task, the network densely self-regularizes the geometric representations needed for pose estimation.

Evaluating a model trained solely on the synthetic SOPE dataset across ROPE (with real scans), real-world datasets HANDAL and HouseCat6D, and real-robot picking experiments, F2G-Pose outperformed the prior state-of-the-art GenPose++ while achieving an ultra-fast real-time inference speed of 28 FPS. The robot arm demonstrated precise, latency-free grasping, showing strong potential as a practical robot perception system.
contributions: Proposed a real-time RGB-D framework that eliminates test-time sampling and intermediate alignment, predicting 6D pose, metric size, and shape completion simultaneously in a single forward pass.
Built a network that efficiently captures diverse intra-category geometric structures by combining DGCNN and an MoE Transformer with foundation feature lifting onto partial point clouds.
Substantially boosted accuracy by jointly learning camera-frame 3D shape completion, providing dense geometric regularization for the pose and size estimation branches.
Achieved state-of-the-art accuracy alongside 28 FPS real-time speed across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, demonstrating real-time pick-and-place manipulation on a physical robot arm.

sections.heading: Why solve it directly in one shot instead of using intermediate representations or diffusion models?
sections.summary: Category-level pose estimation is vital for manipulation, but traditional intermediate alignments suffer from error propagation, and diffusion models incur heavy computational costs and complex post-processing. F2G-Pose resolves this by lifting foundation features and jointly learning shape completion, enabling direct single-pass prediction.
sections.details:
Category-level 6D object pose estimation recovers an object's 3D rotation, translation, and metric size from observed RGB-D data without prior CAD models for specific instances. While essential for robots to dexterously handle everyday items in cluttered environments, it remains an extremely challenging problem with ambiguous solutions due to occlusions, missing depth data, symmetries, and shape variations within the same category.

Conventional deterministic methods predominantly rely on defining a canonical coordinate frame, establishing correspondences with observed points, and then solving for alignment. However, this intermediate representation approach has a major weakness: when occlusions or domain shifts occur, errors in intermediate predictions propagate directly into the final result. Meanwhile, generative approaches using diffusion models (such as GenPose) offer the advantage of modeling pose ambiguities as distributions, but sampling numerous candidates followed by scoring and clustering results in long inference times that cannot match robot control cycles.

In response, the authors propose F2G-Pose, which completely eliminates sampling and directly outputs pose, size, and camera-frame shape in a single feed-forward pass. It binds rich semantic representations from vision foundation models to point clouds, integrating local geometry and global structure for direct regression. By solving shape completion as an auxiliary task, it achieves stable, geometrically consistent direct predictions without relying on intermediate representations.

sections.heading: The evolution of category-level pose estimation and foundation model fusion
sections.summary: Methods have evolved from canonical coordinate systems like NOCS to recent diffusion models. F2G-Pose overcomes both inference latency and error propagation by combining foundation model visual features with point cloud geometry, MoE, and dense geometric supervision via shape completion.
sections.details:
The history of category-level 6D pose estimation gained major traction with NOCS, which defined normalized coordinate spaces for object categories. Since then, many extensions have emerged, such as leveraging point cloud geometry, introducing symmetry-aware loss functions, and fitting shapes with deformation models. However, because these methods heavily rely on intermediate representations, their accuracy drops drastically when observation noise is high.

Recently, diffusion-based methods like GenPose and GenPose++, as well as flow-matching approaches like RFMPose, have been introduced to sample multiple pose candidates. While theoretically sound, they introduce new bottlenecks: the difficulty of candidate extraction (selecting a single final prediction from sampled candidates) and the loss of real-time capability caused by iterative computation.

On the other hand, instance-level pose estimation utilizing CAD models or reference views has successfully leveraged large foundation models, as seen in FoundationPose. In category-level tasks, methods like SecondPose have also begun combining foundation features with geometry. F2G-Pose takes this a step further: it combines the cross-category expressive power of MoE with dense geometric regularization via camera-frame shape completion, achieving both high accuracy and ultra-fast inference.

sections.heading: An integrated design uniting feature lifting, MoE, and shape completion
sections.summary: F2G-Pose projects visual features from RADIOv2.5 onto depth point clouds, extracting global representations via DGCNN and an MoE Transformer. Parallel heads then directly regress pose and size while reconstructing complete point clouds in the camera frame, trained together for geometric consistency.
sections.details:
The inputs are a cropped RGB image $\mathbf{I}$ and a segmented partial point cloud $\mathbf{P}$. The outputs are the 6D pose $\mathbf{T} = (\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}) \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$, the metric size $\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3$, and the completed point cloud $\mathbf{P}_{\text{dense}}$ in the camera frame.

### 3.1 Geometry-Aware Foundation Feature Lifting
First, features are extracted from multiple layers (layers 8, 16, and 23) of a frozen visual foundation model, RADIOv2.5, and fused with convolutional layers to match channel dimensions. RADIOv2.5 combines the fine-grained geometric extraction capability of SAM with the semantic correspondence power of DINOv2. Feature vectors corresponding to the camera-projected coordinates of each 3D point $\mathbf{P}_i$ are sampled from the feature map and attached (lifted). Feeding this point cloud into a Dynamic Graph CNN (DGCNN) to convolve local neighborhood graphs produces 128 object tokens that tightly fuse geometry and semantics.

### 3.2 MoE-Based Object Encoding
The extracted tokens are processed through an 8-layer Transformer. Crucially, the feed-forward network (FFN) in each layer is replaced with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) consisting of 8 experts. Each token is conditionally routed to the Top-2 experts. This allows the network to partition and learn shape variations across 149 diverse categories—from everyday items to tools—without increasing computational cost. A load-balancing loss is also introduced during training to prevent expert collapse.

### 3.3 Direct Pose, Size, and Shape Decoding
Two parallel heads branch from the encoded global representation. The pose and size head predicts rotation using a continuous 6D representation (the first two columns of the rotation matrix), which is converted to $\mathbf{R}$ via Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization. Translation $\mathbf{t}$ and size $\mathbf{s}$ are directly regressed using MLPs. The shape head first generates a coarse point cloud (512 points) from the global features, combines them with sampled observed points, and scores their confidence. By predicting local offsets for surviving points, it produces a dense completed point cloud (2048 points) directly in the camera coordinate frame.

### 3.4 Training Loss Design
A Smooth L1 loss is used for pose and size. For objects with rotational symmetries (90-degree, 180-degree, continuous, etc.), the error is computed against the ground-truth rotation variant closest to the prediction. Chamfer Distance (L1 norm) is adopted for shape completion, matching both coarse and dense point clouds against the ground truth. The model is trained end-to-end with the combined loss including the MoE auxiliary loss.

sections.heading: 28 FPS real-time inference, superior accuracy, and physical robot pick-and-place validation
sections.summary: Trained only on synthetic SOPE data, F2G-Pose outperformed GenPose++ on ROPE (which contains real scans) and achieved 28 FPS inference. Ablations confirmed the contribution of each component, and physical robot picking experiments demonstrated high grasping success rates.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods
The model was trained solely on the synthetic SOPE dataset spanning 149 categories. Evaluations were conducted on synthetic SOPE, ROPE with real scanned objects, the real-world dataset HANDAL, and HouseCat6D containing transparent and reflective items.
As shown in Table 1, F2G-Pose substantially improved performance on ROPE, boosting the IoU50 AUC from GenPose++'s 31.9 to 43.7, while reducing the mean rotation error from $19.9^{\circ}$ to $15.7^{\circ}$. Its inference speed is especially notable: while GenPose++ achieves only 4 FPS due to sampling and post-processing, F2G-Pose runs at 28 FPS in pose-only mode and 24 FPS for the full model including shape completion.
Analyzing why it outperforms diffusion models (Table 2), generative models like GenPose++ do contain excellent solutions among sampled candidates (oracle median of $1.78^{\circ}$), but have heavy tails reaching a mean error of $39^{\circ}$. Consequently, subsequent scoring or clustering suffers from a "candidate-to-decision gap" where incorrect candidates are chosen. F2G-Pose eliminates this gap via direct prediction.

### 4.2 Ablation Study and Robustness
Ablation experiments (Table 4) revealed that removing RADIO foundation feature lifting caused the sharpest performance drop, confirming that visual semantics play a decisive role in pose estimation. Replacing MoE with standard dense FFNs also degraded accuracy, demonstrating the value of MoE for diverse shapes. Furthermore, removing the shape completion auxiliary task reduced pose and size accuracy, proving that dense geometric supervision in the camera frame strongly regularizes the shared representation. Material robustness tests (Table 7) also showed resilience against depth dropouts on transparent and reflective objects.

### 4.3 Real-World Evaluation and Robotic Manipulation
In cross-domain evaluation on the HANDAL dataset (Table 8), F2G-Pose outperformed prior methods (Any6D and GenPose++) under reference-view-free settings.
Finally, real-world pick-and-place experiments were conducted using an ARX robot arm, parallel gripper, and RealSense camera (Figure 4). Testing on randomly placed tableware, bottles, and tools, F2G-Pose achieved 74 grasp successes and 68 placement successes across 80 trials (85% success rate). In real-world environments requiring control cycles within 50 ms, it proved to be a practical solution balancing high precision with real-time speed.

From left to right: input RGB, ground truth (GT), GenPose++, our method (Ours), and completed 3D point clouds in the camera frame predicted by our method on the far right. The method recovers complete shapes from partial point clouds while predicting accurate 3D bounding boxes.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future directions
sections.summary: F2G-Pose successfully achieves category-level 6D pose estimation in real time with high accuracy through foundation feature lifting, MoE, and multitask shape completion. Future work includes addressing dependencies on pre-segmented masks and ambiguities from transparent or tiny objects.
sections.details:
This study presented F2G-Pose, a real-time framework that directly predicts an object's 6D pose, metric size, and completed 3D shape from a single RGB-D observation in one feed-forward pass. By doing away with the iterative sampling used in generative models and combining geometry-aware feature lifting, an MoE Transformer, and dense camera-frame shape completion, it achieved both high accuracy and 28 FPS real-time speed.

The authors note several key limitations, primarily that the system assumes an instance segmentation mask as input during inference. Mask failures or severe depth dropouts adversely affect direct prediction. In addition, perfectly symmetric, textureless objects or severe occlusions can make it difficult to narrow down pose candidates. Future work includes developing an end-to-end framework without external masks, expanding category support to articulated or deformable objects, and integrating active perception to handle heavy occlusions.

sections.heading: Appendix: Robustness stress tests and failure pattern analysis
sections.summary: The appendix details robustness tests under lighting variations and noise, sensitivity to segmentation mask quality, specialization of MoE experts, and typical failure cases caused by reflections and symmetries.
sections.details:
### Robustness and Input Sensitivity Tests
The model showed only mild degradation under harsh photometric perturbations (Figure 5), such as exposure adjustments ($\pm 2.2$ EV) and color temperature shifts ($\pm 4000$ K). In contrast, adding depth noise had a noticeable impact, confirming that depth quality is vital for metric consistency. Additionally, mask erosion degraded performance much more severely than mask dilation (incorporating background), highlighting the critical risk of losing foreground geometric information.

### MoE Expert Routing Analysis
Analyzing token routing across 7,466 samples revealed a significant correlation between categories and expert selection (Cramér's $V = 0.306$). Experts loosely specialized into broad geometric categories such as bag-like, planar, or bowl-like shapes, confirming that the network autonomously learned distinct shape regimes.

### Failure Case Analysis
As shown in Figures 6 and 7, complete depth loss caused by highly reflective surfaces like metallic tableware, or textureless box-shaped objects with bilateral symmetry, can lead to 90-degree or 180-degree flipped pose estimates. In these cases, geometric cues are entirely absent from the observation, leaving multi-view fusion and explicit uncertainty modeling as important future directions.

captions.F5: Examples of input perturbations for robustness evaluation. The top row shows stress tests on RGB images under intense lighting and exposure variations; the bottom row shows heteroscedastic noise injected into depth point clouds.
captions.F6: Failure cases caused by reflective materials. When depth sensor measurements drop out heavily or distort on objects like metallic bowls, correct poses and shapes cannot be reconstructed, leading to rotational errors.
captions.F7: Failure cases on geometrically regular symmetric or small objects. For textureless, highly symmetric objects, determining the principal axis direction remains ambiguous, resulting in 90- or 180-degree pose misorientations.

takeaways: Lifting powerful foundation model features onto geometric point clouds to predict poses directly in one shot is far faster and more reliable for robotics than sampling many candidates with diffusion models and filtering them post-hoc.
In category-level pose estimation, jointly training 3D shape completion in the camera frame as an auxiliary task strongly regularizes shared features, substantially boosting pose and size accuracy.

When handling numerous categories with a single network, replacing Transformer FFNs with MoE (Mixture-of-Experts) effectively expands category- and shape-specific capacity without blowing up inference cost.
limitations: The method assumes pre-segmented object masks (RGB-D crops) as input, meaning upstream segmentation failures directly cause downstream pose estimation errors.
Severe depth dropouts from reflective or transparent materials, as well as thin structures or symmetric low-texture objects, can still lead to 90-degree or 180-degree rotation flips.

Because it relies on single direct regression, the model cannot express multi-modal uncertainty distributions or reject/abstain from predictions when an object's orientation is physically indistinguishable.
